issues.legal_issue: The general law permitting condonation of delay applies to proceedings governed by a special statute that prescribes its own limitation period, where the special statute also makes the general limitation law applicable subject to its own limitation provisions.
material_facts: The governing tenancy law prescribed a 30-day period for applying to set aside an order striking out a tenant’s defence.
The tenant applied after that period had expired and also sought condonation of the delay.
The governing law made the Limitation Act applicable to proceedings under it, subject to its own provisions relating to limitation.
issues.conclusion: The application was barred by the special limitation period, but the tenant’s application for condonation under section 5 of the Limitation Act was maintainable and had to be decided on its merits.
issues.legal_principle: Section 39 of the West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1956 made the provisions of the Limitation Act applicable to proceedings under that Act, subject to the Act’s own limitation provisions. The special period prescribed for the application under section 17A therefore governed, but section 39 did not exclude section 5 of the Limitation Act. The Court approved the view in M/s. Pakarmal Gurudayal v. Sagarmal Bengani, 76 C.W.N. 486.

predicates.special_statute_proceeding: A party brings a proceeding governed by a special statutory scheme.
predicates.special_deadline_prescribed: The special statutory scheme prescribes a specific deadline for the proceeding at issue.
predicates.general_limitation_law_adopted_subject_t: The special statutory scheme makes the general limitation law applicable while giving priority to its own limitation requirements.

issues.definition: When a proceeding under a special statutory scheme is subject to a specific deadline and the scheme otherwise adopts the general limitation law, the general law’s delay-condonation provision applies.

issues.legal_issue: Sufficient cause for a late application to restore a struck-out defence is established when the applicant bona fide pursues a pending revision that could provide effective relief, is delayed by that proceeding, and promptly applies after it is dismissed.
material_facts: The tenant challenged the order striking out his defence by revision, and further proceedings in the eviction suit were stayed while that revision was pending.
The tenant did not apply under the newly introduced remedial provision while pursuing the revision because he was advised incorrectly about the legal position.
The tenant applied under that provision within 30 days after the revision was dismissed.
The Court found that the tenant had acted bona fide and had sufficient cause for missing the prescribed period.
issues.conclusion: The delay was condoned, the application to set aside the order striking out the defence was allowed, and the matter was remitted for the eviction suit to be decided in accordance with law.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 5 of the Limitation Act, 1963, a court may admit a late application if sufficient cause is shown for not filing it within the prescribed period. The Court held that bona fide pursuit of a revision capable of giving effective relief, together with the stay of further proceedings and a prompt application after the revision was dismissed, constituted sufficient cause in this case.

rule.if: application_to_restore_struck_defence and revision_pending_with_proceedings_stayed and bona_fide_pursuit_of_effective_remedy and prompt_application_after_revision_dismissal

predicates.application_to_restore_struck_defence: A party makes a late application seeking restoration of a defence that was struck out.
predicates.revision_pending_with_proceedings_stayed: The party has a revision challenging the striking-out order pending, and further proceedings in the underlying suit are stayed.
predicates.bona_fide_pursuit_of_effective_remedy: The party pursues the revision in good faith because success could provide effective relief, and does not make the restorative application while awaiting its outcome.
predicates.prompt_application_after_revision_dismis: The party makes the restorative application promptly after the revision is dismissed.

issues.definition: A late application to restore a struck-out defence is excused when the applicant in good faith awaits the outcome of a stayed revision that could provide effective relief and applies promptly after that revision is dismissed.

issues.legal_issue: Condoning delay does not enlarge the prescribed limitation period but permits the court to treat the late proceeding as if it had been filed within that period when sufficient cause is shown.
material_facts: The tenant’s application was filed after the prescribed period.
The Court found sufficient cause for the delay because the tenant had bona fide pursued a revision that could provide effective relief and applied promptly after it was dismissed.
issues.conclusion: The delay was condoned by treating the application as if it had been filed within the prescribed period, not by extending that period.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 5 of the Limitation Act, 1963, condonation does not extend the period of limitation prescribed by law. If sufficient cause is shown, the court may treat the proceeding as if it were filed within time.

predicates.late_proceeding: A party files a proceeding after the applicable deadline.
predicates.sufficient_cause_shown: The party establishes a sufficient reason for not filing within the applicable deadline.

issues.definition: A late proceeding is treated as timely when sufficient cause for the delay is shown.
